Discussion 2026-10-25: the brighter-fatter effect, and extrapolating the ramp trend¶

Your two ideas.

  1. Brighter-fatter effect (BFE). "stpsf will not hold for very bright stars, because their PSF core is flattened by the brighter-fatter effect; it should depend on wavelength and differ between NIRCam and MIRI. Can our model take this into account? I added features like the distance to the peak; is that enough?"
  2. Ramp trend. "XGBoost extrapolates the trend from the training set. Can we extrapolate the trend of how the ramp curvature changes with brightness, to predict pixels that saturated even in the first group?"

How they were studied. One agent per idea measured what our data say; a third agent re-checked both reports against the data. The main numbers below come from their output files and were cross-checked in this session.

Short answers¶

your statement verdict in one line
stpsf does not hold for very bright stars right, but mostly for a different reason BFE itself is small (a few %); the large effect is charge that spills out of fully saturated pixels into their neighbours
the core of a bright star becomes flat because of BFE partly BFE makes the star broader with a lower peak; the flat top is saturation
it depends on wavelength and differs between NIRCam and MIRI right larger in NIRCam long wave than short wave; not measurable for MIRI in our data
features like distance to peak let the model learn BFE no the model learns what the labels contain; labels from stpsf contain no BFE, so no feature can add it. The labels must change (done in v5)
XGBoost extrapolates the trend no trees stay flat beyond the brightest training star; the new line + trees model does extrapolate
the ramp-curvature trend predicts first-group-saturated pixels mostly no curvature tells how full a pixel is, not how bright. A pixel saturated in its first read carries almost no flux information in its ramp; its first read (ZEROFRAME) and its star's wings do

Words used here¶

word meaning
full well / saturation level the most charge a pixel can hold (~50,000 DN for NIRCam)
fill how full a pixel is: charge / saturation level
BFE brighter-fatter effect: charge already in a pixel pushes new charge to its neighbours, so bright stars look slightly broader
spill charge that a full pixel cannot hold flows into its neighbours
ZEROFRAME the first read of the detector, 10.7 s after reset; for many saturated pixels it is still below saturation, so it measures their flux
A-hard a pixel saturated even in its first read: it has no usable read at all
ring 1 the 8 pixels touching an A-hard pixel
label the "answer" we train on: the flux from a PSF fit of the star

def end_labels(ax, items, gap=0.07, dx=1.1, log_x=True):
    # name each line at its right end; labels pushed apart so they never overlap
    lo, hi = ax.get_ylim()
    items = sorted(items, key=lambda it: it[1])
    ys = [it[1] for it in items]
    for i in range(1, len(ys)):
        ys[i] = max(ys[i], ys[i - 1] + gap * (hi - lo))
    for (x, y, text), yl in zip(items, ys):
        ax.text(x * dx if log_x else x + dx, yl, text, va='center', fontsize=10, color=INK)

Idea 1: the brighter-fatter effect¶

1.1 Three things that change a bright star's core¶

A schematic of one row of pixels through a star. Bars: charge recorded in each pixel; dashed line: the star's light (what stpsf predicts).

In [2]:
px = np.arange(-5, 6)
light = 100 * np.exp(-0.5 * (px / 1.1) ** 2)                 # the star's light per pixel
bfe = light.copy(); moved = 0.06 * light[5]                    # BFE: the peak pushes a few % of its charge outward
bfe[5] -= moved; bfe[4] += moved / 2; bfe[6] += moved / 2
FULL = 45
sat = np.minimum(light * 3, FULL)                               # a 3x brighter star, recorded with saturation
spill_in = light * 3 - FULL                                     # what the full pixels could not hold
spill = np.minimum(light * 3, FULL).astype(float)
over = np.clip(spill_in, 0, None)
for i in np.flatnonzero(over > 0):                              # half of it lands in the nearest unsaturated neighbours
    for j in (i - 1, i + 1):
        if light[j] * 3 < FULL:
            spill[j] += 0.25 * over[i]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.4), sharey=False)
panels = [(bfe, light, 'Brighter-fatter effect', 'peak a little lower,\nneighbours a little higher\n(a few %)'),
          (sat, light * 3, 'Saturation', 'the top is flat: the pixel\nis full and records nothing more'),
          (spill, light * 3, 'Spill next to full pixels', 'charge a full pixel cannot hold\nflows into its neighbours')]
for ax, (rec, truth, title, note) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.bar(px, rec, width=0.9, color=BLUE, edgecolor='white', linewidth=2)
    ax.plot(np.linspace(-5, 5, 200), np.interp(np.linspace(-5, 5, 200), px, truth), '--', color=INK, lw=1.2)
    if title != 'Brighter-fatter effect':
        ax.axhline(FULL, color=ORANGE, lw=1.5); ax.text(5.6, FULL, 'full', color=INK, va='center')
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel('pixel'); ax.text(0.02, 0.97, note, transform=ax.transAxes, va='top', color=INK, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_ylim(0, (truth.max() if title == 'Brighter-fatter effect' else FULL * 1.6) * 1.15)
axes[0].set_ylabel('charge')
fig.legend(handles=[plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, color=BLUE, label='recorded charge'),
                    Line2D([], [], ls='--', color=INK, label="the star's light (what stpsf predicts)")],
           loc='lower center', ncol=2, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.08))
plt.tight_layout()
  • BFE moves a little charge from the peak to its neighbours while the pixel fills up. The star looks a bit broader, with a slightly lower peak. The core is not flat.
  • Saturation makes the top flat: a full pixel records nothing more. This is the flat core you see in the images.
  • Spill: once a pixel is full, the extra charge has to go somewhere, and part of it ends up in the neighbouring pixels. Those neighbours then record more than the star's light.

1.2 How big is BFE in our data?¶

Unsaturated, isolated stars, measured without any PSF model: the share of a star's light that lands in its brightest pixel, against how full that pixel is. Without BFE the share would stay the same at every fill. Each filter is normalised to its own value at 10-30% fill.

In [3]:
fw = pd.read_parquet(f'{I}/bfe/fwhm_vs_charge.parquet')
fw = fw[fw.inst == 'NIRCAM'].copy()
fw['wave'] = np.where(fw['filter'].str[1:4].astype(int) > 250, 'long wave', 'short wave')
ref = fw[fw.fill.between(0.1, 0.3)].groupby('filter').peakfrac.median()
fw['rel'] = fw.peakfrac / fw['filter'].map(ref) - 1
edges = np.array([0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9])
fw['bin'] = pd.cut(fw.fill, edges)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=1)
labs = []
for (w, g), col, mk in zip(fw.groupby('wave'), [ORANGE, BLUE], ['s', 'o']):
    s = g.groupby('bin', observed=True).rel
    mid = np.array([iv.mid for iv in s.median().index]) * 100
    ax.fill_between(mid, 100 * s.quantile(0.25), 100 * s.quantile(0.75), color=col, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    ax.plot(mid, 100 * s.median(), marker=mk, color=col, ms=8)
    labs.append((mid[-1], 100 * s.median().iloc[-1], f'NIRCam {w} ({s.size().sum():,} stars)'))
ax.set_xlim(15, 115); ax.set_ylim(-12, 6)
end_labels(ax, labs, dx=3, log_x=False)
ax.set_xlabel('how full the brightest pixel is (% of saturation)')
ax.set_ylabel('change in peak-pixel share (%)')
ax.set_title('BFE in unsaturated stars: line = median, band = middle 50%')
Out[3]:
Text(0.5, 1.0, 'BFE in unsaturated stars: line = median, band = middle 50%')

Reading it. From about 20% to 80% fill, the brightest pixel loses about 1% of its share in short wave and about 4% in long wave (medians of thousands of stars; individual filters range from 1-2% and 4-8%). The spread between single stars is larger than the trend, which is why the median of many stars is needed to see it. That is BFE, and it is larger in long wave, as you expected. It is small next to the uncertainty of our labels (0.12-0.21 dex, i.e. 30-60%).

MIRI. The MIRI detectors (Si:As) are known to show a stronger BFE in the literature (Argyriou et al. 2023), but in our data only about 15 isolated MIRI stars span a useful range of fill, and they show no measurable change. An earlier number (20%) came from failed fits of faint stars and does not hold.

1.3 The larger effect: spill next to fully saturated cores¶

For stars with A-hard pixels (saturated even in their first read), compare the label with the ZEROFRAME in two rings: the pixels touching an A-hard pixel (ring 1), and those 2-3 pixels away. A value of 1 means the label and the measured first read agree. Stars are grouped by how many A-hard pixels their core has.

In [4]:
sv = pd.read_parquet(f'{I}/verify/spill_vs_scale_stars.parquet')   # r1, r23: log10(label / ZEROFRAME) per star-exposure
sv['core'] = pd.cut(sv.nhard, [0, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 1e4], labels=['1-2', '3-5', '6-10', '11-20', '21-50', '>50'])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.8), sharey=True)
for ax, det, title in zip(axes, ['SW', 'LW'], ['NIRCam short wave', 'NIRCam long wave']):
    g = sv[sv.det == det].groupby('core', observed=True)
    x = np.arange(g.ngroups)
    for col, name, c, mk in [('r1', 'ring 1 (touching the A-hard core)', ORANGE, 's'), ('r23', 'ring 2-3 px', BLUE, 'o')]:
        ax.plot(x, 10 ** g[col].median(), marker=mk, color=c, ms=8, label=name)
    ax.axhline(1, color=INK, lw=1)
    ax.set_xticks(x, [f'{k}\n({n})' for k, n in g.size().items()])
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel('A-hard pixels in the core\n(number of star-exposures)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('label / ZEROFRAME'); axes[0].legend(loc='lower left')
axes[0].set_ylim(0.3, 1.25)
plt.tight_layout()

Reading it.

  • Ring 1 (orange): the bigger the fully saturated core, the more the touching pixels' first read exceeds the label: by up to x2-3 in long wave for the biggest cores. The extra charge adds up to a sensible fraction (6-38%) of what the core could not hold. This is spill.
  • Ring 2-3 (blue) stays near 1 until the cores are large (more than about 10 A-hard pixels in short wave, 20 in long wave). So a few pixels away, label and measurement agree: the stpsf labels are fine there, and the touching ring is the one that is "wrong" (it holds extra charge, not the star's own light).
  • For the very largest cores, and in short wave for the top 1% of stars, ring 2-3 also drops below 1 (0.7-0.85): there the v4 labels themselves are too low.

What this means for the earlier finding ("labels of the brightest 5% of stars are too low", next_steps_ml_20261023.ipynb): most of that came from ring 1, which holds spilled charge. The labels are too low only for the top ~1% of stars.

1.4 Can a feature like "distance to the peak" teach the model BFE?¶

A toy: the true star has BFE (a slightly broader core); the labels come from a no-BFE PSF fitted to the wings, as ours do. We train a model with the distance to the peak as a feature, on those labels.

In [5]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
r = rng.uniform(0, 4, 20000)
true_prof = lambda r: np.exp(-0.5 * (r / 1.15) ** 2) * 0.92 + 0.08 * np.exp(-0.5 * (r / 2.0) ** 2)   # with BFE: broader core
label_prof = lambda r: np.exp(-0.5 * (r / 1.1) ** 2) * 1.0                                       # no-BFE PSF fitted to the wings
y = label_prof(r) * (1 + rng.normal(0, 0.03, r.size))
m = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.1).fit(r[:, None], y)
grid = np.linspace(0, 4, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
ax.plot(grid, true_prof(grid), color=INK, lw=2.5, label='truth (with BFE)')
ax.plot(grid, label_prof(grid), '--', color=ORANGE, label='labels (no-BFE PSF)')
ax.plot(grid, m.predict(grid[:, None]), ':', color=BLUE, lw=3, label='model trained on the labels,\nwith "distance to peak" as a feature')
ax.set_xlabel('distance to the peak (pixels)'); ax.set_ylabel('flux (peak of labels = 1)')
ax.legend(loc='upper right'); ax.set_title('The model reproduces the labels, not the truth')
Out[5]:
Text(0.5, 1.0, 'The model reproduces the labels, not the truth')

The model follows the labels exactly, because that is what it is trained to do. A feature lets the model use information; it cannot add information the labels do not contain. To include BFE (or spill), the labels must contain it.

1.5 What we do about it¶

step status
Put the measured first reads (ZEROFRAME) of the core into the PSF fit, so the labels follow the real core where it was measured done in v5 (making_training_set.py). On pixels left out of the fit, labels agree better with the first read than v4 labels did (level-1 pixels: +0.005 to +0.034 dex against +0.024 to +0.078; top 1% of stars, 2-3 px ring: -0.075 to -0.04 dex in long wave). Details and caveats in report_v5_20261025.ipynb
Leave the touching ring (ring 1) out of the fit and out of the direct restoration, because it holds spilled charge done in v5 (making_training_set.py, restore_zeroframe.py)
Decide what we restore: the star's light (photon rate), not the charge a pixel happened to collect. For an A-hard pixel only the light is defined (the pixel was full; its extra charge went to the neighbours) adopted; written in the code comments
MIRI: try stpsf blurred by a small extra Gaussian per filter, scored on pixels left out of the fit possible next step
A NIRCam BFE correction kernel; a W51-built PSF per brightness bin not worth it now: BFE is 2-8% against 30-60% label uncertainty, and there are too few isolated bright stars to build brightness-binned PSFs

On ePSFs: they are built from unsaturated stars too, so they would not contain spill or the BFE of very bright stars either. They do not solve this problem.

Idea 2: extrapolating the ramp trend¶

2.1 Does XGBoost extrapolate the trend? No.¶

Take test pixels whose first read measures their flux (A-soft, B, C), and multiply their brightness feature (zeroframe_rate) by 2, 4, ..., 64, keeping everything else fixed. A model that follows the physics should raise its prediction by 0.30 dex (x2) at each doubling. The models were trained on the faintest stars only, so most of the sweep lies beyond anything they have seen.

In [6]:
q = pd.read_csv(f'{I}/ramp/q1_pdp.csv')
q = q[q.sweep.str.startswith('zeroframe_rate')]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.plot(q.factor, 0.301 * q.k, ':', color=INK, lw=1.5)
for col, c, st in [('xgb_dpred', BLUE, 'o-'), ('ridge_dpred', ORANGE, 's--'), ('lin_xgb_dpred', AQUA, 'D-')]:
    ax.plot(q.factor, q[col], st, color=c, ms=7)
# the three rising lines lie on top of each other: one label for them
labs = [(q.factor.iloc[-1], q.ridge_dpred.iloc[-1], 'physics (dotted),\nstraight line (orange)\nand line + trees (aqua)'),
        (q.factor.iloc[-1], q.xgb_dpred.iloc[-1], 'XGBoost')]
first_beyond = q.factor[q.above_train_max > 0.5].min()
ax.axvspan(first_beyond, q.factor.max() * 1.05, color='#f0efec', zorder=0)
ax.text(first_beyond * 1.1, -0.45, 'mostly beyond\nthe brightest training pixel', color=MUTED, fontsize=10)
ax.set_xscale('log', base=2); ax.set_xticks(q.factor, [f'x{f:g}' for f in q.factor])
ax.set_xlim(0.2, 300)
end_labels(ax, labs, gap=0.06, dx=1.15)
ax.set_xlabel('brightness feature multiplied by'); ax.set_ylabel('change of the prediction (dex)')
ax.set_title('Sweeping one brightness feature')
Out[6]:
Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Sweeping one brightness feature')

Reading it. XGBoost (blue) barely moves: +0.05 dex at x32, where the physics says +1.5 dex. A tree model returns the answer of the nearest thing it has seen, so beyond the brightest training pixel it stays flat. The straight line and line + trees follow the physics. This is why the training script now uses line + trees.

2.2 What does the ramp curvature measure?¶

Two pixels, one 10 times brighter than the other. The detector's response bends as a pixel fills (non-linearity). Plotted against time (left), the bright pixel's ramp bends much sooner, so "curvature changes with brightness". Plotted against how full the pixel is (right), both follow the same curve: the bending depends only on the fill. The pipeline's linearity step removes exactly this curve.

In [7]:
FULL = 50000
nonlin = lambda q: q * (1 - 0.12 * (q / FULL) ** 2)     # recorded DN for true charge q (schematic)
t = np.linspace(0, 240, 400)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.8))
for rate, name, c in [(220, 'faint pixel', BLUE), (2200, 'pixel 10x brighter', ORANGE)]:
    q = np.minimum(rate * t, FULL)
    axes[0].plot(t, nonlin(q), color=c, label=name)
    qq = np.linspace(0.01 * FULL, min(rate * 240, FULL), 200)
    axes[1].plot(qq / FULL * 100, nonlin(qq) / np.maximum(qq, 1), color=c, lw=4 if rate < 1000 else 2, label=name)
axes[0].set_xlabel('time since reset (s)'); axes[0].set_ylabel('recorded signal (DN)'); axes[0].set_title('Against time')
axes[1].set_xlabel('how full the pixel is (%)'); axes[1].set_ylabel('recorded / true charge'); axes[1].set_title('Against fill: one curve')
axes[1].set_ylim(0.86, 1.01)
axes[0].legend(loc='lower right'); axes[1].legend(loc='lower left')
plt.tight_layout()

So the "curvature trend" is the rate in disguise: a brighter pixel reaches the bending part sooner. Once a pixel has a straight, unsaturated stretch, its rate is already measured, and the curvature adds nothing.

2.3 What is left for a pixel saturated in its first group?¶

pixel what its own data say
A-soft, B, C (NIRCam) the first read (ZEROFRAME) is below saturation: the flux is measured. No model needed (restore_zeroframe.py)
A-hard, still rising after group 0 the reads still creep up a little before the hard plateau: some information
A-hard, already on the plateau every read sits at the full-well level: only a lower limit ("at least bright enough to fill in 10.7 s")
MIRI level 0 the first read (2.8 s) carries a little information while it is below the ~62k DN ceiling; none at the ceiling

The useful case (A-hard, still rising) disappears exactly where we need it:

In [8]:
c = pd.read_csv(f'{I}/ramp/q2b_climb.csv')
c = c[(c.subset == 'NIRCam A-hard') & (c.by == 'band')].copy()
c['value'] = c.value.astype(float).astype(int)   # the column mixes bands and other groupings, so it loads as text
c = c.sort_values('value')
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.6))
axes[0].bar(np.arange(len(c)), 100 * c.frac_climbing, color=BLUE, edgecolor='white', linewidth=2)
for i, (f, n) in enumerate(zip(c.frac_climbing, c.stars)):
    axes[0].text(i, 100 * f + 2, f'{100 * f:.0f}%', ha='center', color=INK)
axes[0].set_ylabel('A-hard pixels still rising after group 0 (%)')
axes[1].plot(np.arange(len(c)), c.scat_GEO, 's--', color=ORANGE, ms=8)
axes[1].plot(np.arange(len(c)), c.scat_GEO_RAMP, 'o-', color=BLUE, ms=8)
end_labels(axes[1], [(len(c) - 1, c.scat_GEO.iloc[-1], 'star geometry only'), (len(c) - 1, c.scat_GEO_RAMP.iloc[-1], '+ the pixel\'s own ramp')],
           dx=0.15, log_x=False)
axes[1].set_xlim(-0.3, len(c) + 1.2)
axes[1].set_ylabel('error (scatter, dex)')
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(len(c)), ['training\nstars'] + [f'x{2 ** int(v)}' for v in c.value[1:]])
    ax.set_xlabel('star brightness band')
axes[0].set_title('Pixels with ramp information'); axes[1].set_title('A-hard error with and without the ramp')
plt.tight_layout()

Reading it. In the faintest band every A-hard pixel is still rising after group 0, and the ramp helps a little. In the brightest band only about a fifth are, and the pixel's own ramp improves the error by only ~0.03 dex. For the brightest stars, the information about an A-hard pixel comes from the rest of the star: its unsaturated wings and the shape of its saturated region. That is what the PSF fit and the geometry features use.

2.4 Neighbouring pixels¶

Pixels next to a saturating pixel do receive extra charge later in their ramp (their late slopes are 14% higher than their early slopes, against 3% for other pixels). But the extra charge records when the neighbour filled up, not how bright it is (correlation with the neighbour's brightness at most 0.24). It is the same spill as in section 1.3, and it cannot measure the saturated pixel's flux.

2.5 Your idea, corrected¶

Trends that do hold at any brightness, and that we use:

  1. flux = charge / time for any read below saturation. That is the ZEROFRAME restoration for A-soft, B and C pixels.
  2. the time a pixel takes to saturate brackets its flux: a pixel saturating in group k is between "fills by group k" and "fills by group k-1". For a pixel saturated in its first read this gives only the lower limit (the floor).
  3. the shape of the star does not change with brightness, only its height (apart from the few-% BFE). The unsaturated wings set the height, and the PSF gives the core. That is the PSF fit behind the labels, and the geometry features of the model.
  4. a model with a straight-line part continues a trend beyond its training range; trees alone do not. The training script now uses line + trees.

Trends that do not hold: the curvature or creep of saturated reads (beyond the "still rising" case), a tree model's learned trend past its training range, and the extra charge in neighbouring pixels.

Summary of what changed in the code¶

  • making_training_set.py: the first reads (ZEROFRAME) of NIRCam pixels without a pipeline value (level 0 A-soft/B/C, level 1) are fitted as data, except the ring touching an A-hard core (spill); v5 output.
  • restore_zeroframe.py (new): restores NIRCam A-soft/B/C level-0 pixels from the first read, with no model, leaving A-hard pixels and their touching ring for the model.
  • assemble_training_set.py: drops 3x3 junk; matches stars within 1".
  • train_model.py: line + trees model with a calibrated uncertainty band; the brightness-band test replaces the brightest-20% test; also scored against the first read and the floor.

Results of the v5 run: report_v5_20261025.ipynb.
